questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Classify a physical measurement by its level of measurement
questions.stem: A beekeeper's logbook records hive weight in kilograms to the nearest 0.1, counts of frames, and a rating of colony temperament on a four-point scale. Which level of measurement does the weight entry represent?

options.text: Ratio, because zero kilograms means an empty hive and equal differences carry equal meaning
Interval, because the kilogram scale has no true zero point in hive weighing
options.misconception: Denies a true zero to any physical scale

options.text: Ordinal, because heavier hives are ordered but the gaps are not meaningful
options.misconception: Treats a metric scale as a ranked list

options.text: Nominal, because the weight figure only labels which hive was heaviest
options.misconception: Confuses a recorded quantity with a category label

questions.explanation: Kilograms have a meaningful zero and equal differences mean equal added weight, so the entry is ratio level. The tempting error is to assume that because weights are ordered, the scale is only ordinal.
questions.hint: Ask whether zero means the absence of weight.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Separate reliability from validity using a repeated reading
questions.stem: A beekeeper's spring scale reads the same jar of honey as 3.2 kg on every weighing over five days, but the actual jar holds 3.9 kg. What can be concluded about this scale?

options.text: It is reliable but not valid, since it repeats itself yet misses the true value
It is valid but not reliable, since the true value lies within the range it reports
options.misconception: Confuses consistency with accuracy

options.text: It is neither reliable nor valid, since a constant reading cannot be trusted at all
options.misconception: Assumes a repeatable but wrong reading is worthless

options.text: It is both reliable and valid, because five identical readings confirm the weight
options.misconception: Treats repeated identical readings as proof of accuracy

questions.explanation: Repeating the same value shows consistency, which is reliability, while the 0.7 kg shortfall shows it misses the truth, which is lack of validity. A scale can be perfectly repeatable and still be badly wrong.
questions.hint: Ask whether it agrees with itself and with the truth.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: State the evidence that would demonstrate criterion validity
questions.stem: A beekeeper's varroa counting method is compared against alcohol-wash counts taken by a county inspector. Explain what evidence would show the counting method has criterion validity.

answer.exemplar: Criterion validity is shown when the counting method agrees with the independent standard of the alcohol wash across many hives, with a high correlation and small average differences. Evidence should cover hives with genuinely different infestation levels, since agreement only on lightly infested colonies would not demonstrate predictive use.

questions.explanation: Criterion validity asks whether a measure agrees with an accepted outside standard, here the alcohol wash. Agreement across many infestation levels demonstrates it, not one lucky hive.
questions.hint: Compare the method against an independent gold standard.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Convert a validity coefficient into shared variance
questions.stem: A beekeeper rates colony strength on a 0 to 10 scale and the ratings correlate 0.90 with an expert panel's ratings. What percentage of the variation in the scale's ratings is shared with the expert panel?
questions.explanation: Shared variation is the square of the correlation, 0.90 squared is 0.81, so 81 percent of the variation is shared. Reading the correlation as the shared proportion overstates the overlap.
questions.hint: Square the correlation coefficient to get shared variance.

options.text: Two counts a week apart, then minutes apart, then a season apart, then across a requeening
options.misconception: Treats a week apart as more reliable than minutes apart

options.text: Two counts across a requeening, then a season apart, then a week apart, then minutes apart
options.misconception: Ranks a requeening as the most stable condition to measure

questions.explanation: Test-retest reliability is highest when little can change between the two measurements. Minutes apart the colony is identical, while a requeening or a nectar flow changes the quantity measured.
questions.hint: Ask how much the hive could change between tests.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a confounded reading from evidence in an instrument log

options.misconception: Blames the weighing schedule instead of the instrument's drift

options.text: The 0.4 kg offset is small enough that it explains all of the autumn difference
options.misconception: Assumes the measured offset alone explains the seasonal pattern

questions.explanation: The scale reads high on a warm July day and a warm autumn, so warmth and weight are confounded in its output. The fix is calibrating against a known mass at the same temperature.
questions.hint: Ask what else changes the reading besides the hive.

questions.explanation: Calling ventilation wonderful and saying bees improved put the answer inside the question. A neutral stem with a rating scale lets agreement and disagreement both be expressed.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a drifting instrument can still be useful
questions.stem: A beekeeper's hive-scale readings drift a little on each visit, yet the readings are still useful for spotting a sudden swarm. Explain why this tool can be useful despite being unreliable.

answer.exemplar: Unreliable means the readings do not repeat exactly, which is true when the scale drifts slightly and the hive is handled differently each time. Useful does not require exact repeatability: the drift is small compared with the large weight change caused by a swarm, so the measure still detects the event the beekeeper cares about.

questions.explanation: Reliability is about repeating the same value, while usefulness here rests on detecting a large change against small drift. The measure need not be exact to be informative about big swings.
questions.hint: Ask whether the drift is small beside the effect detected.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage error of an instrument against a reference
questions.stem: A beekeeper's sugar-water refractometer reads 1.048 for a syrup batch that the county inspector's calibrated instrument reads as 1.052. What is the percentage error of the refractometer in this reading?
questions.explanation: The absolute difference is 0.004, and dividing by the reference value of 1.052 gives 0.0038, or 0.38 percent. Reporting only the raw difference hides how small the error is.
questions.hint: Divide the absolute difference by the reference reading.

The measure has low reliability because the hives were actually in different condition on Sunday

options.text: The scale is unreliable because the ratings were recorded on different days of the week

options.misconception: Reads a small drift as evidence of strong reliability

questions.explanation: The hives barely changed but the ratings moved, so the difference came from the rater rather than the colonies. Test-retest reliability concerns consistency when the measured object is stable.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why changing scale format changes reported averages
questions.stem: A beekeeper's survey asks beekeepers to rate colony defensiveness on a scale from minus five to plus five and then from zero to ten. Why do the two versions produce different averages for the same hives?

options.text: Different label sets and formats let respondents map their own meaning onto the numbers
The minus five to plus five version is objective while the zero to ten version is subjective
options.misconception: Claims one format is objective and the other purely subjective

options.text: Only the zero to ten scale produces a normal distribution of responses from a colony
options.misconception: Confuses response scale design with the distribution of scores

options.text: The two versions differ because the same colonies were rated at different times of day
options.misconception: Attributes a design effect to timing of the rating

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why ordinal labels cannot be averaged as if they were measurements
questions.stem: A beekeeper records colony strength as 'weak', 'moderate' or 'strong'. Explain why these labels cannot support arithmetic such as averaging a strength score across hives.

answer.exemplar: The three labels are ordinal: they order hives from weak to strong but the gaps between the categories are not known to be equal, so the distance from weak to moderate cannot be assumed to equal that from moderate to strong. Any average or difference computed from the codes treats those arbitrary steps as real quantities and therefore misrepresents the colonies.

questions.explanation: Ordinal labels set an order but not equal steps, so an average of the codes assumes distances the data do not support. Coding the categories as 1, 2 and 3 and treating them as measurements is the trap.
questions.hint: Ask whether the gap between neighbouring labels is known.

questions.hint: Count the exact matches and divide by the total.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a forced-choice scale shapes response patterns
questions.stem: A beekeeper's rating scale offers 'completely disagree' through 'completely agree' with all five points left unlabelled except the two ends. Explain how a forced-choice scale changes the answers.

answer.exemplar: When only the two endpoints are labelled, middle positions mean whatever the respondent supposes they mean, so people place themselves according to their own reading rather than a common standard. Responses then cluster at the ends because the middle feels vague and unattractive, which flattens the apparent distribution and makes disagreement look more common than it is.

questions.explanation: Unlabelled middle points invite each reader to invent a meaning, and people avoid options that feel undefined. Labelling every point with a descriptive anchor makes the scale comparable across beekeepers.
questions.hint: Ask what an unlabelled middle point means to each reader.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain when averaging repeated counts is defensible
questions.stem: A beekeeper's varroa counts on the same board differ by two or three mites each time she counts it. Explain why her counts should not simply be averaged without further thought.

answer.exemplar: Two observers counting the same board will rarely agree exactly, because mites move and some drop off the sticky surface, so each count carries counting error as well as true variation. Averaging counts is appropriate only if the errors are unbiased and independent across repeats, and if the true count is stable in the moment. If counts drift with temperature, mite activity or the board's handling, the spread reflects real change as well as error.

questions.explanation: Repeating a count on a moving board mixes real change with counting error, so a spread of two or three mites is not purely noise. Averaging is defensible only when the true count is stable across repeats.
questions.hint: Ask whether the board's true content changed between counts.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Separate repeatability noise from a systematic personal drift
questions.stem: Two beekeepers use the same scale and the same method on the same hive and get 44.2 kg and 44.9 kg. Later the first beekeeper's readings drift by about 0.2 kg per week. What does this pattern suggest?

options.text: The beekeeper's readings have become less reliable over time, even though the method has not changed
The scale has drifted, since both beekeepers should have obtained identical readings
options.misconception: Attributes a personal drift to a shared instrument

options.text: The method is unreliable, since the two readings on one hive differed by 0.7 kg
options.misconception: Calls ordinary repeatability a method failure

options.text: The hive is changing, since its weight must have moved between the two weighings
options.misconception: Explains two different readings as a change in the object

questions.explanation: Two people following the same procedure on one hive differ slightly, which is ordinary, while the first beekeeper's weekly drift points to their own readings. That is a change in reliability, not in method or hive.
questions.hint: Separate the small repeat difference from the weekly trend.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why validating against another instrument is insufficient
questions.stem: A beekeeper's honey moisture meter is validated against a laboratory refractometer. Explain why validating the meter against another instrument does not by itself make it fit for measuring moisture.

answer.exemplar: A second instrument is only a useful standard if it is itself accurate and free from its own errors, otherwise the comparison simply transfers the reference instrument's faults to the meter. Validation should use a method traceable to a physical definition, check the full working range, and report the size of disagreement across that range so users know when the meter can be trusted.

questions.explanation: Agreement with another device establishes validity only if that device is a sound standard, otherwise errors are copied not checked. Validity also depends on the range tested and the size of disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reference instrument is itself trusted.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Convert a validity correlation into shared variance
questions.stem: A beekeeper's strength rating correlates 0.80 with an expert panel's ratings for the same 25 hives. What is the percentage of shared variance between the two ratings?
questions.explanation: Shared variance is the square of the correlation, and 0.80 squared is 0.64, so 64 percent of the variation is shared. Reading the correlation as the shared proportion overstates the agreement.
questions.hint: Square the correlation to get the shared variance.
